cards.front: Which antitussive is the standard reference drug, and how does it act?
cards.back: Codeine (methylmorphine) is the reference antitussive: more selective for the cough centre than morphine, it suppresses cough for about 6 hours, and naloxone blocks this, showing an opioid-receptor action in the brain. The antitussive dose is lower than the analgesic dose. Constipation is the main drawback; abuse liability is low but real. It depresses breathing at higher doses, so avoid it in asthma, poor respiratory reserve and children. About 10% is O-demethylated to morphine by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers get unexpectedly high morphine levels (dangerous via breast milk), while poor metabolisers get little analgesia. Morphine itself is unsuitable because of addiction and respiratory depression.

cards.front: Dextromethorphan: mechanism, advantages over codeine and important interaction
cards.back: A synthetic central antitussive that blocks NMDA receptors and does not act on mu-opioid receptors; the d-isomer is antitussive (the l-isomer is analgesic). It is about as potent as codeine against cough but has no analgesic action, does not impair mucociliary function and hardly constipates, with fewer GI and subjective side effects. Though regarded as non-addicting, it is abused by some. Side effects: dizziness, nausea, drowsiness. It inhibits neuronal serotonin uptake, so it must be avoided with MAO inhibitors (serotonin syndrome). Not advised below 6 years.

cards.front: Noscapine: what kind of antitussive is it, and what is the caution in asthma?
cards.back: A non-narcotic opium alkaloid of the benzoisoquinoline series. Its antitussive potency is close to codeine, but it has no narcotic, analgesic or dependence-producing action; it is especially useful in spasmodic cough. It can release histamine, so it may provoke bronchoconstriction in asthmatics. Headache and nausea occur occasionally.

cards.front: When is an antitussive justified, and why should a productive cough not be suppressed?
cards.back: Justified for dry, non-productive cough, or when cough disturbs sleep or is hazardous (hernia, piles, cardiac disease, after eye surgery). A productive cough clears airway secretions, so suppressing it can retain secretions and is harmful.

cards.front: How does bromhexine act as a mucolytic, and what is its active metabolite?
cards.back: It depolymerises mucopolysaccharide chains directly and also by releasing lysosomal enzymes, which breaks up the fibre network of tenacious sputum. It is derived from vasicine, an alkaloid of Adhatoda vasica. Its metabolite ambroxol has a similar action.

cards.front: Why should inhaled salbutamol not be used on a regular schedule?
cards.back: Inhaled salbutamol acts within minutes and lasts only 2 to 4 hours, so it is a reliever, to be used as required by symptoms rather than on a regular schedule. Regular use can lead to receptor down-regulation and tolerance and may worsen bronchial hyperreactivity; rising use signals that more anti-inflammatory therapy is needed. GINA now advises that every asthmatic, however mild, should get inhaled corticosteroid at least each time a bronchodilator is used, and GG14 notes that ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue bronchodilator of choice because it avoids the dangers of SABA overuse.

cards.front: Compare salmeterol and formoterol as long-acting beta-2 agonists.
cards.back: Both last about 12 hours and are given twice daily for maintenance. Salmeterol is a partial agonist with a slower onset, so it is not used for relief; its long aliphatic side chain is thought to anchor it near the receptor. Formoterol is an almost full agonist with a rapid onset, so combined with an inhaled corticosteroid it can also be used as the reliever. In asthma a LABA must never be used alone, because it does not treat inflammation and may increase the risk of life-threatening and fatal attacks; it is given with an ICS, preferably in one combination inhaler.

cards.front: What are the main mechanisms by which theophylline helps asthma and COPD?
cards.back: Non-selective, weak inhibition of phosphodiesterases (PDE3 and PDE4 matter most), which raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial muscle and damps inflammatory cells. It also blocks adenosine receptors, and adenosine A1 blockade is implicated in toxic arrhythmias and seizures. At low concentrations it may enhance histone deacetylation, which suppresses inflammatory gene transcription.

cards.front: Why does theophylline have a narrow safety margin and non-linear kinetics?
cards.back: The safety margin is narrow: dose-related toxicity begins in the upper part of the therapeutic range (KDT: 5 to 20 µg/mL; GG14 now regards 5 to 15 mg/L as therapeutic, since anti-inflammatory benefit occurs below 10 mg/L). Metabolism, mainly by CYP1A2, is saturable, so at higher doses kinetics change from first to zero order, the half-life lengthens (up to about 60 hours) and plasma levels rise out of proportion to dose. Clearance varies widely between patients (age, smoking, heart failure, liver disease, interacting drugs), so only sustained-release preparations are used, to avoid high peaks.

cards.front: Name drugs that lower and drugs that raise theophylline levels, and the dose response for each.
cards.back: Lower (CYP1A2 inducers): smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbitone; the dose must be increased. Raise (CYP inhibitors): erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives, allopurinol; the dose is reduced to about two-thirds. Theophylline itself potentiates furosemide, sympathomimetics, digitalis, oral anticoagulants and hypoglycaemics, and reduces the effects of phenytoin and lithium.

cards.front: What is the role of inhaled corticosteroids in asthma, and when do they act?
cards.back: Inhaled corticosteroids suppress bronchial inflammation and hyperreactivity, improve peak flow, reduce the need for rescue beta-2 agonist and prevent acute episodes. They have no role during an acute attack or status asthmaticus. Peak effect is seen after 4 to 7 days (KDT), though maximal effect on airway hyperresponsiveness may take several weeks or months (GG14); benefit persists for a few weeks after stopping. GINA recommends ICS for all asthmatics, however mild, at least on an as-needed basis with each bronchodilator dose. Systemic effects are clinically relevant only above about 600 µg/day (KDT).

cards.front: Omalizumab: what is it, how does it work, and in which patients is it used?
cards.back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against IgE, given subcutaneously every 2 to 4 weeks; the dose is set by the circulating total IgE level. It neutralises free IgE, so little is left to bind the high-affinity receptor (FcεRI) on mast cells, and mediator release on allergen challenge falls; it also lowers FcεRI expression and circulating IgE. Used in severe allergic (extrinsic) asthma, where it reduces exacerbations, including virus-induced ones, and steroid needs. No benefit in non-allergic asthma; very expensive.

cards.front: Montelukast and zafirlukast: mechanism, role and limitations.
cards.back: Competitive antagonists at the cysLT1 receptor, reducing bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leakage and eosinophil recruitment. Taken orally. Used as alternative or add-on controllers in mild-to-moderate asthma, particularly aspirin-induced and exercise-induced asthma; they are less effective than even low-dose ICS and are not for acute attacks or COPD. Generally well tolerated, but headache and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis are reported, and montelukast now carries an FDA black-box warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts.

cards.front: Sodium cromoglycate: mechanism, uses and why it fails in an acute attack.
cards.back: A chromone that stops mast cells degranulating, limiting release of histamine, leukotrienes and PAF. It is not a bronchodilator and does not block constrictor agonists, so it is useless during an attack. Oral absorption is negligible, so it is inhaled, and benefit takes 2 to 4 weeks. Used prophylactically in extrinsic and exercise-induced asthma, and in allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis.

cards.front: Short note: Management of acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus)

points: High-flow oxygen; rapid assessment of severity; alert the intensive care unit if features of impending respiratory failure
Nebulised SABA (salbutamol) is the bronchodilator of choice; the nebulised route is safer than and as effective as IV
Add nebulised ipratropium: additive with the beta-2 agonist
Parenteral (SC/IM) salbutamol or terbutaline only if inhaled drug cannot reach the airways
IV hydrocortisone (GG14: 4 mg/kg, then 3 mg/kg 6-hourly) or methylprednisolone; onset takes several hours
Oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg is about as effective as IV hydrocortisone and easier to give
IV or nebulised magnesium sulphate helps severe exacerbations in adults and children
IV aminophylline: KDT regards routine use as outmoded; if used, GG14 gives 6 mg/kg over 20 to 30 min then 0.5 mg/kg/h, halved if the patient already takes theophylline
Correct dehydration and acidosis; watch for hypokalaemia from beta-2 agonists
Treat chest infection with antibiotics when present
Intubation and mechanical ventilation if the patient fails to respond

cards.front: Short note: Inhalation devices for asthma

points: Aerosols deliver drug to the airway, so less drug is needed and systemic effects fall
Only about 10 percent of an inhaled dose reaches its site of action
Uses HFA propellant; CFC propellants are banned
Needs coordination of actuation with a deep breath, which many patients cannot manage
Removes the need for precise coordination
Large particles settle on its walls, reducing oropharyngeal deposition and swallowed dose
Reduces local effects such as candidiasis with inhaled steroids
Portable; capsule is punctured and powder is released by inspiratory flow
Needs a strong inspiratory effort, so unsuitable for children, the elderly and the very sick
Can irritate the airway and provoke cough
Jet or ultrasonic; preferred for severe attacks, children and the elderly
Can deliver more than one drug at once; used at the bedside

cards.front: Short note: Stepwise pharmacological management of asthma

points: Treatment is matched to severity and level of control; step up for poor control
Step down gradually once asthma is controlled for about 3 to 6 months
Inhaled route preferred; ICS is the anti-inflammatory foundation
Step 1, mild episodic: inhaled SABA at each episode only
Step 2, mild persistent: regular low-dose ICS (leukotriene antagonist or theophylline less satisfactory)
Step 3, moderate: low-dose ICS plus LABA, or medium-dose ICS alone
Step 4, severe: high-dose ICS plus LABA, with leukotriene antagonist or SR theophylline added
Step 5: oral corticosteroid, at the lowest dose, with attempts to withdraw

sections.h: Newer approach (GINA, as in Katzung and GG14)
points: All asthmatics, however mild, should receive ICS at least on an as-needed basis, every time a bronchodilator is taken; guidelines still differ on this
ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue inhaler of choice, avoiding the dangers of SABA overuse
LABA always combined with ICS, preferably in one inhaler
LAMA (tiotropium) added to ICS-LABA
Low-dose azithromycin reduces exacerbations
Biologics by phenotype: anti-IgE, anti-IL-5/IL-5R, anti-IL-4R, anti-TSLP

cards.front: Short note: Management of cough by its cause

points: Upper or lower respiratory tract infection: appropriate antibiotics
Pulmonary tuberculosis: antitubercular drugs
Smoking, chronic bronchitis or bronchiectasis: stop smoking, avoid pollutants, steam inhalation and postural drainage
Asthmatic cough: inhaled beta-2 agonist, corticosteroid or ipratropium
Eosinophilic lung disease: diethylcarbamazine with inhaled corticosteroid
Postnasal drip from allergic rhinitis or sinusitis: antihistamine, nasal steroid, decongestant or antibiotic as indicated
Avoid the precipitating allergen
Gastro-oesophageal reflux: head-of-bed elevation, light dinner, H2 blocker or proton pump inhibitor
ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker
Post-viral cough needs no specific treatment and subsides by itself

cards.front: Short note: Beta-2 agonists in asthma

points: Stimulate beta-2 receptors, raising cAMP in bronchial smooth muscle and relaxing it; also inhibit mediator release
Selective beta-2 agents cause fewer cardiac effects than isoprenaline or adrenaline
Salbutamol and terbutaline: onset within minutes, action 2 to 4 hours
Relievers, used as required; not for regular use
Salmeterol: slower onset, partial agonist, about 12 hours, twice daily
Formoterol: rapid onset, near-full agonist, about 12 hours; can be used as reliever with an ICS
Once-daily agents (indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol) act over 24 hours; mainly COPD; fluticasone furoate/vilanterol is used in asthma and COPD
Muscle tremor is commonest; tachycardia and palpitation
Hypokalaemia; tolerance of non-airway responses with continuous use
Never use a LABA alone in asthma; always with an ICS
Cautions: hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, digitalis therapy

cards.front: Short note: Anticholinergic bronchodilators

points: Block muscarinic (M3) receptors that mediate vagal bronchoconstriction
Act mainly on larger airways, which carry vagal innervation
Short-acting: ipratropium, about 4 to 6 hours
Long-acting (LAMA): tiotropium, glycopyrronium and umeclidinium once daily; aclidinium twice daily
Poorly absorbed when inhaled, so few systemic effects; dry mouth and bitter taste
Reflex cholinergic tone is a major reversible component, so LAMAs are the bronchodilators of choice in COPD in preference to LABAs alone
Tiotropium improves lung function and reduces exacerbations; LABA/LAMA combination inhalers add benefit
Less effective and slower than beta-2 agonists
LAMA (tiotropium) is an add-on for asthma not controlled on ICS-LABA
Nebulised ipratropium with salbutamol in acute severe asthma
Nebulised ipratropium can precipitate glaucoma in the elderly; use a mouthpiece rather than a face mask

cards.front: Essay: Bronchial asthma: pathogenesis and the rationale for drug treatment

points: Asthma is reversible airway obstruction from hyperresponsiveness
Symptoms: dyspnoea, wheeze, cough and limited activity
Extrinsic (episodic, allergic) and intrinsic (perennial, prone to status asthmaticus) forms
Mast cells start the process; eosinophils, lymphocytes and mast cells dominate the infiltrate
Chronic inflammation leads to remodelling and worsens hyperreactivity
TSLP from airway epithelium drives type 2 (eosinophilic) inflammation through TH2 and ILC2 cells; IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 and TSLP are now targets of biologics
Stored mediators released at once: histamine, proteases, TNF
Newly synthesised mediators within minutes: prostaglandins, leukotrienes, PAF
Gene-driven cytokines over hours: interleukins and TNF
Prevent antigen-antibody reaction; neutralise IgE
Suppress inflammation; prevent mediator release
Antagonise mediators; block constrictor nerves; mimic dilator nerves
Beta-2 agonists and anticholinergics for bronchodilatation
Corticosteroids, mast cell stabilisers, leukotriene antagonists and anti-IgE for inflammation
Methylxanthines as adjuncts with weaker, less predictable effects
Escalate with severity and step down after control
GINA now advises ICS for all asthmatics, at least as needed with each bronchodilator dose
Inhalation route favoured to limit systemic side effects

cards.front: Essay: Inhaled corticosteroids in asthma

points: Asthma is an inflammatory disease, so anti-inflammatory therapy is central
Inhaled steroids give local action with little systemic effect
Beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone, mometasone and ciclesonide
Beclometasone dipropionate and ciclesonide are prodrugs activated by lung esterases
Budesonide, fluticasone and mometasone have high first-pass metabolism, so fewer systemic effects
No role in an acute attack or status asthmaticus
Peak effect after 4 to 7 days (KDT); maximal effect on hyperresponsiveness may take weeks to months (GG14)
Benefit persists for some weeks after stopping
Start at an appropriate dose and reduce to the lowest that maintains control
Doses are classed as low, medium or high, and differ between drugs and between MDI and dry powder devices
Local: hoarseness, dysphonia, sore throat, oropharyngeal candidiasis
Reduced by spacers and by gargling after each dose
Systemic effects (adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, cataract, growth delay) mainly above about 600 µg a day
Asthma: controller therapy for persistent asthma; GINA now recommends ICS for all asthmatics, at least as needed
COPD: inflammation is relatively steroid-resistant; ICS mainly reduce exacerbations in patients with frequent exacerbations and blood eosinophils above 300/µL
High-dose ICS raise the risk of pneumonia in COPD (more with fluticasone than budesonide)

cards.front: Essay: Theophylline: mechanism, toxicity, interactions and therapeutic role

points: Methylxanthine related to caffeine and theobromine
Once central to asthma therapy, now limited by a narrow safety margin
CNS stimulation and vomiting; cardiac stimulation and tachycardia
Vasodilatation; diuresis; relaxation of all smooth muscle, most marked in bronchi
Increased gastric acid and pepsin secretion and gastric irritation
Non-selective PDE inhibition raises cAMP
Adenosine receptor blockade, implicated in toxic arrhythmias and seizures
Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum needs very high concentrations
Well absorbed orally; about 50 percent protein bound; metabolised by CYP1A2
Half-life about 7 to 12 hours in adults; shorter in children and longer in the elderly
Saturable metabolism: half-life rises and levels increase out of proportion to dose
Lower doses needed in age over 60, heart failure, pneumonia and liver failure
Therapeutic range narrow: book 5 to 20 µg/mL; many current guidelines aim for 5 to 15 µg/mL
Therapeutic range: KDT 5 to 20 µg/mL; GG14 now 5 to 15 mg/L
Toxicity starts in the upper therapeutic range; children are more prone to CNS toxicity
Rapid intravenous injection can cause collapse, arrhythmia or asystole
Enzyme inducers lower levels; enzyme inhibitors raise them
Theophylline potentiates digitalis, furosemide and anticoagulants
Now restricted to COPD and selected asthma as an adjuvant, e.g. nocturnal asthma
Apnoea of prematurity; caffeine is equally effective
IV aminophylline in status asthmaticus is regarded as outmoded

cards.front: Essay: Antitussives, expectorants and mucolytics: rational use

points: Cough is protective: it clears secretions and foreign particles
Useless or non-productive cough is the target for suppression
Opioid: codeine (standard), morphine (too addictive), ethylmorphine, pholcodine
Non-productive or troublesome cough is the target for suppression
Peripheral: prenoxdiazine desensitises pulmonary stretch receptors
Antihistamines relieve cough by sedation but do not suppress it selectively
Expectorant evidence is weak; steam inhalation and hydration may help more
Mucolytics: bromhexine and ambroxol depolymerise mucopolysaccharides
Acetylcysteine opens disulfide bonds; carbocisteine is an oral option
Useful in tracheostomy, cystic fibrosis and thick mucus plugs
Many are irrational and offer mainly placebo effect
Bronchodilators and antihistamines in combination act with differing time courses
Fixed-dose combinations of a central antitussive with a bronchodilator or with a strongly anticholinergic antihistamine are banned in India, yet many such products remain on sale
Treat the underlying cause such as infection, asthma, reflux or ACE inhibitor use
Antitussives are symptomatic only and should be used for limited periods

cards.front: Classify: antitussives
cards.text: Opioid antitussives: {{codeine}} is the standard; {{morphine}} is most effective but unsuitable. Nonopioid central agents: {{noscapine}}, {{dextromethorphan}} and {{chlophedianol}}. Peripheral agent: {{prenoxdiazine}}, which desensitises pulmonary stretch receptors.

cards.front: Classify: beta-2 agonists by duration
cards.text: {{Salbutamol}} is a short-acting selective agonist acting for 2 to 4 hours; {{salmeterol}} is a long-acting agonist given {{twice daily}} with slow onset; {{formoterol}} has a faster onset and acts for about {{12 hours}}; {{indacaterol}} is an ultra-long-acting agent given {{once daily}} in COPD.

cards.front: Classify: antiasthma drugs by class
cards.text: Methylxanthine: {{theophylline}}. Muscarinic antagonist: {{ipratropium}}. Mast cell stabiliser: {{sodium cromoglycate}}. Cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonists: {{montelukast}} and {{zafirlukast}}. 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor: {{zileuton}}. Anti-IgE antibody: {{omalizumab}}.

cards.front: Classify: theophylline drug interactions
cards.text: CYP1A2 inducers such as {{smoking}}, {{phenytoin}} and {{rifampicin}} lower theophylline levels, so the dose must rise. Inhibitors such as {{erythromycin}}, {{ciprofloxacin}} and {{cimetidine}} raise levels, so the dose is cut to about {{two-thirds}}.

cards.front: Classify: aerosol particle size and deposition
cards.text: Particles of {{1 to 5 micrometres}} reach the bronchioles; larger particles settle in the {{oropharynx}}; very fine particles are {{exhaled}}. Only about {{10 percent}} of an inhaled dose reaches the site of action. A {{spacer}} lets larger particles settle out, reducing swallowed dose and {{candidiasis}}.

cards.front: Classify: leukotriene and mast cell pharmacology
cards.text: Cysteinyl leukotrienes act on the {{cysLT1}} receptor; {{zileuton}} blocks {{5-lipoxygenase}} but is limited by {{hepatotoxicity}}; cromoglycate {{stabilises}} mast cells and is {{not}} a bronchodilator.

cards.front: Short note: Biologics for severe asthma

points: Severe asthma uncontrolled despite high-dose inhaled therapy
Choice depends on phenotype: allergic (high IgE) or eosinophilic type 2 inflammation (blood eosinophils above 300/µL)
Omalizumab: severe allergic asthma; SC every 2 to 4 weeks, dose by IgE level
Mepolizumab (SC every 4 weeks) and reslizumab (IV every 4 weeks) block circulating IL-5
Benralizumab (SC every 8 weeks) blocks IL-5R and causes eosinophil apoptosis
Dupilumab (SC every 2 weeks) blocks signalling by both IL-4 and IL-13; for eosinophilic or steroid-dependent asthma; also atopic dermatitis and nasal polyposis
Can cause peripheral eosinophilia, usually transient
Tezepelumab blocks the epithelial alarmin TSLP; works in eosinophilic and also non-type 2 asthma; approved from 12 years
Anti-IL-5 drugs cut exacerbations by about half and reduce oral steroid dose by at least 50%

cards.front: Why is ICS-formoterol now preferred over a SABA alone as the reliever in asthma?
cards.back: Formoterol has a rapid onset, so unlike salmeterol it can relieve symptoms, and each reliever dose of the combination also delivers inhaled corticosteroid when symptoms flare. GG14 states that ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue bronchodilator of choice, being more effective and avoiding the dangers of SABA overuse. GINA (cited in Katzung) advises that all asthmatics, however mild, take ICS at least whenever a bronchodilator is used, because even mild asthma carries a risk of life-threatening attacks; other guidelines do not all agree.

cards.front: Roflumilast: mechanism, use and adverse effects
cards.back: An oral PDE4 inhibitor given once daily, converted by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to the more active N-oxide metabolite; it exerts an anti-inflammatory action mainly in the lungs rather than direct bronchodilation. Used as add-on therapy in severe COPD (FEV1 below 50%) with chronic bronchitis and frequent exacerbations, reducing exacerbations by about 20% with little effect on symptoms; not approved for asthma. Adverse effects: diarrhoea (commonest), nausea, headache, weight loss and psychiatric disturbances. CYP inhibitors raise and rifampicin lowers its levels; contraindicated in moderate-to-severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh B or C).

cards.front: Short note: Drug therapy of stable COPD

points: Progressive airflow limitation from noxious particles, chiefly cigarette smoke; may progress even after exposure stops
Inflammation is relatively resistant to corticosteroids
LAMAs (tiotropium, glycopyrronium, umeclidinium, aclidinium) are bronchodilators of choice in preference to LABAs alone
Once-daily LABAs (indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol); LABA/LAMA combination inhalers improve lung function over either alone
Reserved for frequent exacerbators with blood eosinophils above 300/µL, usually as ICS/LABA/LAMA triple inhalers
Increase pneumonia risk
Roflumilast for severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and exacerbations
Daily azithromycin reduces exacerbations
Theophylline: low-dose trial showed no reduction in exacerbations; limited by toxicity
Managed much as in asthma (bronchodilators, systemic steroids), plus routine antibiotics such as beta-lactams, doxycycline or azithromycin against H. influenzae
A short 1 to 3 week course of oral glucocorticoid may help (KDT)
